hints: At the interior maximum, differentiate $5\sin2x\cos^2x$ with the product and chain rules and set the derivative to zero.
After factoring common trigonometric terms, use double-angle identities to reduce the condition to one function, such as an equation in $\tan^2x$.
Solve on $0\le x\le\pi/2$ and compare with the zero-valued endpoints to select the exact maximum coordinate.
walkthrough:
Rewrite $y = 5\sin(2x)\cos^2 x$ in terms of single-angle functions using $\sin(2x) = 2\sin x\cos x$:
$$y = 5(2\sin x\cos x)\cos^2 x = 10\sin x\cos^3 x$$

Differentiate with respect to $x$ using the product rule:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 10\left[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\sin x) \cdot \cos^3 x + \sin x \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\cos^3 x) \right]$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\sin x) = \cos x$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\cos^3 x) = 3\cos^2 x(-\sin x) = -3\sin x\cos^2 x$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 10[\cos^4 x - 3\sin^2 x\cos^2 x] = 10\cos^2 x(\cos^2 x - 3\sin^2 x)$$

Set $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$ to find the stationary points:
$$10\cos^2 x(\cos^2 x - 3\sin^2 x) = 0$$

Solve in the interval $0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $\cos x \neq 0$:
$$\cos^2 x - 3\sin^2 x = 0$$
$$3\sin^2 x = \cos^2 x$$
$$\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x} = \dfrac{1}{3} \implies \tan^2 x = \dfrac{1}{3}$$

Take the square root, noting $\tan x > 0$ for $x \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$:
$$\tan x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$
$$x = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

ai_rubric.Finding Stationary Points: Set derivative zero and derives one trig function. The solved value is x=π/6.

hints: With $u=\cos x$, use $du=-\sin x\,dx$ and change the limits: $x=0$ gives $u=1$, while $x=\pi/4$ gives $u=1/\sqrt2$.
Account for the reversed limits or the minus sign, integrate the resulting cubic in $u$, and simplify the exact area.
walkthrough:
Set up the definite integral for the area under $y = 5\sin(2x)\cos^2 x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\text{Area} = \int_0^{\pi/4} 5\sin(2x)\cos^2 x\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^{\pi/4} 10\sin x\cos^3 x\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Apply the substitution $u = \cos x$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = -\sin x \implies \sin x\,\mathrm{d}x = -\mathrm{d}u$$

Change the limits of integration:
$$\text{When } x = 0: \quad u = \cos(0) = 1$$
$$\text{When } x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}: \quad u = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$

Substitute into the integral and use the negative sign to invert limits:
$$\text{Area} = \int_1^{1/\sqrt{2}} 10u^3(-\mathrm{d}u) = \int_{1/\sqrt{2}}^1 10u^3\,\mathrm{d}u$$

Evaluate at the limits:
$$\text{At } u = 1: \quad \dfrac{5}{2}(1)^4 = \dfrac{5}{2}$$
$$\text{At } u = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}: \quad \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^4 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} \implies \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{5}{8}$$
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{5}{2} - \dfrac{5}{8} = \dfrac{20}{8} - \dfrac{5}{8} = \dfrac{15}{8}$$

ai_rubric.Integration by Substitution: Du/dx=−sinx. Applies u=1 at x=0 and u=1/√2 at x=π/4 in Cu⁴ or Ccos⁴x. The final result is 15/8.
